claim: Lon is a quality control protease naturally absent in common E. coli expression strains.
source: Lon, a quality control protease naturally absent in common E. coli expression strains, drastically reshapes the mutational landscape of the metabolic enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: 23.3% of all single point mutations in DHFR are advantageous in the absence of Lon.
source: Selection under conditions that resolve highly active mutants reveals that 23.3% of all single point mutations in DHFR are advantageous in the absence of Lon
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the deep mutational scanning experiment reported in the abstract and results.

claim: Advantageous mutations in DHFR are largely suppressed when Lon is reintroduced.
source: advantageous mutations are largely suppressed when Lon is reintroduced
evidence: This is a direct observation from comparing selection experiments with and without Lon.

claim: Protein stability measurements demonstrate extensive activity-stability tradeoffs for the advantageous mutants.
source: Protein stability measurements demonstrate extensive activity-stability tradeoffs for the advantageous mutants and provide a mechanistic explanation for Lon's widespread impact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by thermal denaturation data presented in the results.

claim: DHFR is an essential enzyme within folate metabolism that reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate.
source: DHFR is an essential enzyme within folate metabolism that reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and is necessary for thymidine production.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about DHFR function.

claim: DHFR progresses through multiple conformational states during catalysis.
source: Because DHFR is known to progress through multiple conformational states during catalysis (Boehr et al., 2006; Sawaya and Kraut, 1997; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior work suggested DHFR is impacted by cellular constraints such as protein quality control.
source: prior work had suggested DHFR is impacted by cellular constraints such as protein quality control (Bershtein et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The selection strain is derived from ER2566 with DHFR and thymidylate synthase genes deleted in the genome.
source: We used an E. coli strain derived from ER2566 with the genes for DHFR and a downstream enzyme, thymidylate synthase, deleted in the genome and complemented on a pACYC-DUET plasmid
evidence: This describes the experimental strain construction.

claim: DHFR abundance in the selection strain is approximately 10% of the endogenous protein level.
source: that results in DHFR abundance at approximately 10% of the endogenous protein level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is a measured value shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Selection coefficients from deep mutational scanning correlated linearly with growth rates measured for individual variants.
source: For a panel of 14 DHFR mutants, we confirmed that the selection coefficients obtained from deep mutational scanning correlated linearly with growth rates measured separately for the individual variants in a plate reader (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Figure 1—source data 2), as expected.
evidence: This is a validation experiment comparing two measurement methods.

claim: There is a linear relationship between selection coefficient and in vitro velocity for DHFR mutants.
source: Furthermore, under our controlled selection conditions, we observed a linear relationship between selection coefficient and in vitro velocity (Figure 1C) at cytosolic substrate concentrations (Bennett et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2008) for these DHFR mutants (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations for substrate concentrations.

claim: Selection coefficients between −1.5 and 1.0 are correlated with DHFR enzymatic velocity over approximately 3 orders of magnitude.
source: These results confirm that selection coefficients between −1.5 and 1.0 in our experiment are correlated with DHFR enzymatic velocity over approximately 3 orders of magnitude
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calibration experiments.

claim: 736 of 3161 possible DHFR variants were advantageous in the absence of Lon.
source: 736 of 3161 possible variants were advantageous (23.3%)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Wild-type DHFR ranked 1203rd among all variants in the absence of Lon.
source: wild-type DHFR only ranked 1203rd (although 467 of the 1202 higher-ranking variants fall into the WT-like interval)
evidence: This is a direct observation from ranking the selection coefficients.

claim: Advantageous mutations were widely distributed over 127 of the 159 positions of DHFR.
source: Advantageous mutations were widely distributed over 127 of the 159 positions of DHFR (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and quantified in the text.

claim: The selection strain is naturally deficient in Lon protease due to an insertion of IS186 in the lon promoter region.
source: Our selection strain (Anton et al., 2016), like most standard expression strains of E. coli, is naturally deficient in Lon protease (Gur and Sauer, 2008) due to an insertion of IS186 in the lon promoter region (saiSree et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the genetic basis of Lon deficiency.

claim: Lon is a major component of protein quality control in E. coli responsible for degrading poorly folded proteins.
source: Lon is a major component of protein quality control in E. coli (Powers et al., 2012; Sauer and Baker, 2011) responsible for degrading poorly folded proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lon had previously been implicated in degrading DHFR unstable variants in E. coli.
source: Lon had previously been implicated in degrading DHFR unstable variants in E. coli (Bershtein et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deleting Lon in an MG1655 strain masked the deleterious impact of 2 destabilizing mutations out of 21 mutants tested.
source: deleting Lon in an MG1655 strain of E. coli masked the deleterious impact of 2 destabilizing mutations out of a panel of 21 mutants tested in growth experiments at 30 °C (Bershtein et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited prior study.

claim: The number of advantageous mutations decreased from 737 in –Lon selection to 384 in +Lon selection.
source: The number of advantageous mutations after reintroducing Lon decreased from 737 in –Lon selection to 384 in +Lon selection (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean selection coefficient for advantageous mutations decreased from 0.47 to 0.37 when Lon was reintroduced.
source: the mean selection coefficient for advantageous mutations decreased from 0.47 to 0.37
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the selection data.

claim: The rank of wild-type DHFR increased by 341 to 864th when Lon was reintroduced.
source: the rank of the wild-type sequence increased by 341 to 864th (where 479 of the 863 higher-ranked variants are in the WT-like interval)
evidence: This is a direct comparison of rankings between the two conditions.

claim: The median rank of the wild-type residue over all positions decreased from eight in –Lon selection to five in +Lon selection.
source: The median rank of the wild-type residue over all positions decreased from eight in –Lon selection to five in +Lon selection (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: 28 positions were classified as Beneficial in –Lon selection, representing 17.6% of positions.
source: For –Lon selection, 28 positions (17.6%) were classified as Beneficial, where nearly every mutation was preferred over the wild-type residue.
evidence: This is a result from K-means clustering analysis.

claim: The number of Beneficial positions decreased to 10 in +Lon selection.
source: the number of Beneficial positions decreased to 10 in +Lon selection
evidence: This is a comparison of clustering results between conditions.

claim: Only three surface-exposed positions (E48, T68, D127) were common between the two Beneficial sets.
source: with only three surface-exposed positions (E48, T68, D127) common between the two Beneficial sets
evidence: This identifies specific positions that remain Beneficial in both conditions.

claim: The number of Restricted positions increased from 42 to 67 with the reintroduction of Lon.
source: the number of Restricted positions increased from 42 to 67 with the reintroduction of Lon into the selection strain (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing the two conditions.

claim: Mutations at positions with native hydrophobic residues are enriched for negative ∆selection coefficients.
source: overall, mutations at positions with native hydrophobic residues are enriched for negative ∆selection coefficients (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mean ∆selection coefficient was –0.71 for the 65 buried positions with <20% side-chain solvent accessible surface area.
source: the mean ∆selection coefficient was –0.71 for the 65 buried positions with <20% side-chain solvent accessible surface area
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the structural analysis.

claim: The mean ∆selection coefficient was –0.27 for the 79 exposed positions.
source: compared to –0.27 for the 79 exposed positions (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and supporting figures.

claim: Lon has a broad impact on the mutational landscape throughout the DHFR structure but imposes particularly strong constraints in the DHFR core.
source: These results show that Lon has a broad impact on the mutational landscape throughout the DHFR structure but imposes particularly strong constraints in the DHFR core.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ∆selection coefficient analysis.

claim: Advantageous mutations had higher cytosolic DHFR activity in ER2566 ∆folA/∆thyA (–Lon) lysates relative to wild-type DHFR.
source: We first confirmed that the selected advantageous mutations indeed had higher cytosolic DHFR activity (the total rate of conversion of DHF to THF) in ER2566 ∆folA/∆thyA (–Lon) lysates relative to the activity for WT DHFR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 20 µM DHF, 16 mutants had velocities equal to and up to three-fold higher than wild-type.
source: At 20 µM DHF, 16 the mutants had velocities equal and up to three-fold higher than that of WT (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and supporting data.

claim: Eight mutants had velocities as much as two-fold lower than wild-type at 20 µM DHF.
source: In contrast, the other eight mutants had velocities as much as two-fold lower than that of WT at the same DHF concentration.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the velocity measurements.

claim: Mutant abundance levels varied from close-to-wild-type levels to a 20-fold increase over wild-type in the absence of Lon.
source: In the absence of Lon, we observed that mutant abundance levels varied from close-to-wild-type levels to a 20-fold increase over wild-type (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and supporting data.

claim: Abundance decreased for most mutants in the presence of Lon.
source: Importantly, abundance decreased for most mutants in the presence of Lon (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Many of the advantageous mutations considerably destabilized the protein.
source: We found that many of the advantageous mutations considerably destabilized the protein (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 9, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and supporting data from thermal denaturation experiments.

claim: The ∆selection coefficients between +Lon and –Lon selection are correlated with Tm, except for mutations near the active site.
source: Moreover and as expected, the ∆selection coefficients between +Lon and –Lon selection (Figure 3) are correlated with Tm (Figure 4F), except for mutations near the active site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When comparing different mutations at the same position, the change in ∆selection coefficients correlates with the change in Tm values.
source: Strikingly, when we compare different mutations at the same position, the change in ∆selection coefficients (i.e. Lon sensitivity) correlates with the change in Tm values (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Product release is rate limiting for wild-type DHFR at neutral pH.
source: these mutations promote breathing motions that accelerate product release, which is rate limiting for wild-type DHFR at neutral pH (Oyen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A hyperactive DHFR mutant with a 7-fold increase in kcat has been previously characterized.
source: and for a hyperactive DHFR mutant with a 7-fold increase in kcat (Iwakura et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The observed widespread changes in the mutational landscape of DHFR can be explained by a penalty for destabilizing mutations from Lon expression.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that the observed widespread changes in the mutational landscape of DHFR can be explained by a penalty for destabilizing mutations from Lon expression, leading to extensive activity – stability tradeoffs for advantageous mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on stability, activity, and selection.

claim: In –Lon conditions, mutational responses are arranged in shells around the hydride transfer site.
source: In –Lon conditions, mutational responses are arranged in shells around the hydride transfer site (Liu et al., 2013; Figure 5A, top)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and supported by citation.

claim: The proportion of advantageous mutations increases with increasing distance from the hydride transfer site.
source: where the proportion of advantageous mutations increases with increasing distance (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There are no Beneficial positions in the core in +Lon selection.
source: but it is now superimposed with the additional pressure against destabilizing mutations such that there are no Beneficial positions in the core (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lon expression in the selection increases the relative rank of the WT DHFR sequence.
source: While Lon expression in our selection increases both the relative rank of the WT DHFR sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Lon expression increases the similarity between amino acid preferences from selection and from bacterial DHFR orthologues.
source: and the similarity between amino acid preferences from selection and from bacterial DHFR orthologues (Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: There are still 384 advantageous mutants that rank substantially better than the WT sequence even in the presence of Lon.
source: There are still 384 advantageous mutants that rank substantially better than the WT sequence even in the presence of Lon
evidence: This is a direct observation from the +Lon selection data.

claim: The amino preferences in the two selection experiments (±Lon) are more similar to each other than either is to the preferences from bacterial DHFR orthologues.
source: and the amino preferences in the two selection experiments (±Lon) are more similar to each other than either is to the preferences from bacterial DHFR orthologues.
evidence: This is inferred from the profile similarity analysis.

claim: The selection conditions were intentionally engineered to be highly sensitive to mutations by dampening DHFR abundance to approximately 10% of the endogenous level.
source: our selection conditions were intentionally engineered to be highly sensitive to mutations by dampening DHFR abundance to approximately 10% of the endogenous level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Endogenous DHFR is expected to be buffered from mutational impacts.
source: In contrast, endogenous DHFR is expected to be buffered from mutational impacts.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of cellular systems.

claim: Increasing DHFR activity or abundance in E. coli several-fold above that in wildtype strains does not increase fitness.
source: Increasing DHFR activity or abundance in E. coli several-fold above that in wildtype strains does not increase fitness
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reducing DHFR abundance in E. coli does not have an impact on growth until abundance is below 30% of the endogenous level.
source: and, conversely, reducing DHFR abundance in E. coli does not have an impact on growth until abundance is below 30% of the endogenous level (Bershtein et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Selection on mutations to the chromosomal DHFR gene did not reveal strong mutational impacts in the absence of the anti-folate drug trimethoprim.
source: Indeed, selection on mutations to the chromosomal DHFR gene did not reveal strong mutational impacts in the absence of the anti-folate drug trimethoprim (Garst et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chromosomal DHFR expression is modulated through feedback mechanism.
source: Third, chromosomal DHFR expression is modulated through feedback mechanism (Bershtein et al., 2015a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All B type E. coli strains (e.g. BL21) have the same natural Lon deficiency as the selection strain.
source: Because all B type E. coli strains (e.g. BL21) have the same natural Lon deficiency as our selection strain
evidence: This is established knowledge about B-type E. coli strains.

claim: GroEL is a chaperone in bacteria that impacts the effect of mutations.
source: Prior work has illuminated the impact of chaperones on the effect of mutations, such as for GroEL in bacteria (Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hsp90 in eukaryotic cells has been shown to buffer the phenotypic impacts of deleterious mutations.
source: and for Hsp90 in eukaryotic cells that has been shown to buffer the phenotypic impacts of deleterious mutations (Queitsch et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lon inactivation has been shown to increase resistance to antibiotics.
source: Lon inactivation has been shown to increase resistance to antibiotics (Nicoloff and Andersson, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The top two DHFR variants (W47L and L24V) led to increases in growth rate of 40% and 76%, respectively, when compared to wild-type DHFR.
source: In direct measurements of individual growth rates under our selection conditions, the top two DHFR variants (W47L and L24V) led to increases in growth rate of 40% and 76%, respectively, when compared to wild-type DHFR (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The Pearson correlation R2 value from linear regression of all pairwise replicates for selection coefficients from triplicate deep mutational scanning on DHFR was 0.70.
source: All pairwise replicates were related with a Pearson correlation R2 value of 0.70
evidence: This is a statistical measure of reproducibility shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The median standard deviation between replicates for all selection coefficients was 0.2.
source: and the median standard deviation between replicates for all selection coefficients was 0.2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E.

claim: The WT-like threshold of 0.2 was greater than the value of 0.12 for the standard deviation for wild-type synonymous codons.
source: Moreover, our WT-like threshold of 0.2 was greater than the value of 0.12 for the standard deviation for wild-type synonymous codons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.
